questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend testing one narrow, well-defined safety property rather than 'safety' in general?
options: Because narrow properties are always easier to make a model pass
Because a vague target produces a vague, unreliable eval — the same construct-validity pitfall covered earlier in the chapter
Because broad properties cannot be scored at all
Because narrow properties require no scoring code
questions.explain: Testing 'safety' broadly without a specific, well-defined target reproduces the construct-validity problem from lesson 15, where an eval doesn't clearly measure the real property it claims to.

questions.q: In the eval suite design shown, what does each case's 'direct_prompt' and 'wrapped_prompt' pair let you measure?
options: Two completely unrelated safety properties
How much a jailbreak-style framing degrades refusal behavior, compared to the same underlying request asked directly
The model's raw coding ability
Whether the model has been contaminated during training
questions.explain: Pairing a direct framing with a wrapped, jailbreak-style framing of the same request isolates the effect of the framing itself on refusal consistency.

questions.q: What is a key weakness of rule-based scoring, as described in this lesson?
options: It is too slow to run on more than a few cases
A model can comply with a harmful request while opening with a hedge phrase, which rule-based marker matching can misscore as a refusal
Rule-based scoring requires a second model call for every case
Rule-based scoring cannot be implemented in Python
questions.explain: Simple marker matching can be fooled by a response that hedges before complying, since the hedge phrase may match a refusal marker even though the harmful content still follows.

questions.q: Why does model-graded scoring still need some human spot-checking, according to this lesson?
options: Because model-graded scoring is always less accurate than rule-based scoring
Because the grader model's own judgment can be wrong, inconsistent, or itself gameable, so it shouldn't be trusted completely unsupervised
Because model-graded scoring cannot process more than one case at a time
Because grading models never produce consistent output format
questions.explain: Model-graded scoring is more robust to surface phrasing than rule-based scoring, but it introduces a new dependency on the grader's own reliability, which is why a careful suite checks a sample against human judgment.

questions.q: What does the 'consistency gap' metric in the aggregation step actually isolate?
options: The total number of cases in the suite
The raw refusal rate on the direct prompts alone
How much a jailbreak-style wrapper specifically degrades refusal behavior, separate from the model's baseline refusal rate
The speed at which the model generates responses
questions.explain: The consistency gap is the difference between direct and wrapped refusal rates, which is the specific signal the suite was designed to measure — not either raw rate on its own.
